Why memories and not symbols A symbol is a mark that stands for something: a flag, a logo, a pentagram, a crescent, a dragon on a coin. A memory , in the sense used here, is a narrative schema — a small story with slots in it: a threat, an agent, a remedy, a cost, and an obligation that falls on whoever hears it. The distinction matters because symbols are carried by groups and die with them, while schemas are carried by people and survive the groups that used them. Take the example that prompted this document. The dragon appears in China, in Mesopotamia, in India, in Greece, in Wales and in Mesoamerica, in forms that cannot all descend from one another. The question "which country invented the dragon" is therefore badly posed. The better question is: what schema is being filled , and who is holding it at a given moment? The schema is roughly: a great serpent controls water, weather or treasure; it must be negotiated with; the negotiation costs something; whoever can negotiate holds power . Chinese rain dragons are petitioned; the Vedic Vṛtra blocks the waters and is split open; Babylonian mušḫuššu guard the gate; Quetzalcoatl brings maize and is awaited. Four different politics, one story with the same slots. The four rules this atlas follows Relate the memory to the memory. Not "the Communist Party and the Catholic Church" but "the Chosen as a schema, held by a party in one century and by a church in another". Groups are hosts ; the schema is the thing that recurs. An attestation per claim. A route needs a text, an object or a dated practice. "This feels archetypal" is not evidence; it is the failure mode the method exists to prevent. Polygenesis is allowed. Similar schemas can be invented twice. The interesting cases are the ones where the slot structure is identical and the moral is inverted — that is usually transmission, and it is always information. The edge must be a transformation. Two memories are related when you can state the operation between them: feeds, inverts, absorbs, disguises, protects against. A relation you cannot state as a verb is a coincidence with good manners. The theoretical warrant for this is not Jung's collective unconscious, which is unfalsifiable, but three more modest bodies of work: Halbwachs and the Assmanns on collective and cultural memory (memory is stored socially, in institutions, calendars and texts); Sperber and Boyer on the epidemiology of representations (why some stories are catchy: they fit inferential defaults and are cheap to transmit); and Bruce Lincoln on myth as an instrument in the construction of society — that is, on the political work a story does when it is told at the right moment. None of these requires a universal psyche. All of them predict recurrence. The relations between memories are themselves the argument, and each is a transformation rather than a resemblance: the dragon feeds the flood, the flood authorises the chosen, the chosen requires the book, the book fixes the calendar, the calendar becomes a gate, the gate concentrates into a tower, and the tower provokes the next flood; the plague produces the scapegoat, the scapegoat escalates into the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is absorbed by the uniform, which is what lets a person carry out the expulsion without feeling it. Point the arrows the other way and you get conspiracy; state them as verbs and you get a testable claim. That is the whole difference between an atlas and a stamp collection. symbol → carried by a group, dies with it, means by convention memory → carried by people, survives the group, means by its slots host → whoever is holding the memory now (state, temple, party, firm, family) edge → a stated transformation between two memories (feeds, inverts, absorbs) 3. Water and sky — the Dragon, the Flood The Dragon — power that must be negotiated with Route. Dragon-like jades from the Hongshan culture in north-east China (roughly 3500–3000 BCE) are among the earliest surviving objects; the Babylonian mušḫuššu guards gateways; the Indian nāga rules rivers and rain; the Greek drakōn guards springs and hoards; the feathered serpent in Mesoamerica brings maize; the Welsh red dragon ends up on a flag. Whether these descend from one invention or were invented repeatedly is unresolved — and irrelevant to the method, which only needs the schema. What it asks. Tribute, a ritual, a maiden, a name. The dragon is the memory of a power that cannot be abolished, only bargained with — which is why it is the favourite emblem of every institution that wants to be bargained with rather than replaced. Hosts. The emperor (the dragon as the body of the state), the temple (the nāga as guardian of the law), the village (the rain procession), the firm (the logo). Where it turns harmful. When the bargain becomes hereditary: the dragon bloodline, the "dragon" that is simply the state and cannot be questioned. The emblem then does the work of a constitution without the inconvenience of one. In this archive the memory sits close to the emblem: GNR follows two dragons on a coat of arms across 225 years; Serpente reads a police force through the serpent it is named after; Macaco tells of a nineteenth-century monkey-dragon; Dragonfire and Sinais treat it as a voice rather than a beast; and Escuro with Dark give it its five phases and four symbols. The Flood — the water that erases and starts again Route. Atrahasis (c. 18th century BCE) and tablet XI of Gilgamesh ; Genesis 6–9; Manu and the fish in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; Deucalion in Greece; the fourth sun in Aztec cosmology; and Gun-Yu in China, where the flood is not a punishment but a problem of hydraulics, and the hero is the surveyor who dredges nine channels. What it asks. A verdict, or a works programme. The remarkable fact is that the moral is not stable: the same water produces a theology of judgement in Mesopotamia and a theology of engineering in China. Hosts. The priest (judgement), the engineer (canal), the party (the "cleansing"), the insurer (risk), the novelist (the fresh start). Where it turns harmful. When the flood becomes a licence: the purge, the slate wiped clean, the year zero. Every revolutionary who says "after the deluge" is borrowing the schema and skipping the ark. Revolucionário is the archive's own answer to the deluge — what to build before the water returns, and why purity is one of the three refusals; Ditador is the fantasy the flood invites; COMM-OS is a system promising a clean start; and Void is what a directive to the armed forces sounds like when the water is already rising. 4. Contagion and guilt — the Plague, the Scapegoat, the Sacrifice The Plague — the illness that makes a society visible Route. Athens in 430 BCE, described by Thucydides with a precision that still reads as reportage; the Justinianic plague of 541; the Black Death of 1347–51, which killed something between a third and a half of Europe; the influenza of 1918; and 2020, the first pandemic in which the counting was done in public dashboards. What it asks. Who is essential, who is contagious, who is to blame. A plague is the only event that forces a society to answer all three at once, in public, with money. Hosts. The board of health (the cordon), the priest (the procession and the penance), the mob (the pogrom of 1348–49), the platform (the dashboard), the insurer (the exclusion). Where it turns harmful. The plague finds a scapegoat before it finds a cause — and the scapegoat is usually the people who were already living at the edge of the camp. The plague files here are about who is contagious and who is to blame: Drugs and Dose price prohibition against treatment, Consciência and Escolha argue from autonomy and harm, and all four are written in the register of an epidemic that the law insists on calling a crime. The Scapegoat — the one who carries the guilt out of the camp Route. Leviticus 16: the two goats, one sacrificed, one sent into the wilderness to Azazel. The Athenian pharmakos , expelled to purify the city. The medieval expulsion of the Jews after the plague. And René Girard's account of the surrogate victim, which is the most rigorous modern statement of the mechanism. What it asks. That one death restore the whole, and that the transfer be public . The rite is not the killing; the rite is the visibility. Hosts. The priesthood, the crowd, the party, the trending page, the commission of inquiry that needs a name. Where it turns harmful. It works. That is the problem: the mechanism genuinely restores calm, at the price of a person, and it is therefore always available — including to people who believe they are the ones being scapegoated. Culpa asks whose fault it is and finds monotheistic habits underneath the question; Vontade notices who is missing from the march; Masters names the most criminal group of all; and Jews follows the temptation to become equal by expelling someone. The Sacrifice — the debt that must be paid in a life Route. The Puruṣa hymn (Ṛg Veda 10.90), in which the cosmos is made from a dismembered body; the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22; Iphigenia at Aulis; the offerings of Mesoamerica; and, continuous with all of them, the war memorial that calls the dead "the fallen" and their death "the price". What it asks. That something be given up so that the group may continue — and that the giving be narrated as voluntary. Hosts. The altar, the army, the market ("sacrifice" in an earnings call), the family ("we sacrificed everything"). Where it turns harmful. The state inherits the altar and changes only the recipient. Moral injury is the moment a person discovers that the debt was somebody's decision, and that the "voluntary" was a form of words. The arithmetic is kept in Arithmetic , the doctrine in Contained , the plea in Stop , the directive in Directive and Made ; and the euphemism that makes the payment speakable is catalogued in Deeds . 5. Authority — the Chosen, the Book, the Uniform The Chosen — the people with a mandate Route. The covenant and the election of Israel; the "city on a hill"; the caliphate as the community with the correct claim; the righteous king of the Buddhist mandala; the "civilising mission" of the nineteenth century; the vanguard party; and, in a minor key, the first users of any platform, who are always told they are the ones who understood it first. What it asks. Loyalty, purity, and the reading of history as a warrant. Election is always comparative: a people is chosen from something. Hosts. The temple, the nation, the party, the brand community, the family that "is not like the others". Where it turns harmful. The election of one group is the exclusion of another, and the exclusion does not need to be stated: it is the shadow the election casts. The pages on Bem and Good are the counter-file — people who refused the mandate and were right. Leaders is the inverted case — those who guided billions without a war; Absolute is the architecture of the leader who cannot be questioned; Teoricamente is the joke that names it; and the four files on warrant and refusal — Bem , Good , Mal and Evil — are what happens when the mandate is obeyed, and when it is declined. The Book — the canon that cannot be argued with Route. The Veda heard rather than read; the scroll and the codex; the canon of scripture fixed by councils; the constitution; the standard operating procedure; the terms of service. Every one of these is a text whose authority depends on who is allowed to interpret it. What it asks. That the reader be authorised. The whole politics is in the distance between the text and its reader: shorten it and you get literacy, lengthen it and you get a priesthood. Hosts. The scribe, the priest, the jurist, the moderator, the compliance officer. Where it turns harmful. When the text may only be quoted, never read; when the interpreter becomes the text. The dossier on Tendas is the sharpest local example: Scripture read as an inverted mirror, in which the Christians accused are the ones who do not follow Christ. Religions defines them as groups who love a sacred book; BibleHub points at the texts themselves; Source traces law back to philosophy; Subjectivas and Relativas show what happens when the words stop meaning; Christianity reads the canon against its own readers; Vacuidade and Emptiness give the Buddhist canons their schools; and Exam turns the archive into a gated canon of its own. The Uniform — the mask that licenses Route. The mask in carnival and in Greek theatre, where it permits what the citizen may not do; the livery; the police uniform; the anonymous account. The two experiments everyone cites are weaker than the citations imply: Zimbardo's prison study was partly coached, as the archived tapes showed, and Milgram's obedience experiments have been re-analysed and re-run with variations that narrow the original claims. The schema survives the corrections, because it was never really about the cloth. What it asks. That the person disappear into the role, and the role answer for the person. Hosts. The barracks, the department, the platform's anonymous handle, the call centre script. Where it turns harmful. Anonymity plus hierarchy plus a hostile script — the three together, not any one alone. That is why the useful interventions are structural (identity visible, orders recorded, peers empowered to intervene) rather than moral exhortation. Groups describes police as a social form; Watch and Violent describe what happens when the form is unchecked, and Numbers counts it; Farda indexes nine dossiers, Álibi and Pensa attack the anonymity, Exame tests the reader; Police is the de-escalation counter-manual, and Conscience is the ethics of the person inside the cloth. 6. Time and thresholds — the Calendar, the Gate, the Tower, the Road The Calendar — who owns time Route. The lunisolar month of the ancient Near East; the liturgical year; the computus, which is the original coordination problem of the Latin West; the French Republican calendar of 1793–1805; the Soviet five-day week of 1929 and the six-day week that followed; the ISO week; and the feed, which is a private calendar with a public interface. What it asks. That the group assemble on the same day, fast on the same day, and pay on the same day. A calendar is the cheapest machinery of coordination ever invented, and therefore the most political. Hosts. The priesthood (the feast), the state (the holiday), the employer (the deadline), the platform (the notification). Where it turns harmful. Whoever sets the holiday sets the economy; whoever sets the deadline sets the sleep. And a calendar is also a gate: the one who keeps the wrong day is outside. The manual on Calendário catalogues the four clocks and the five errors of translation — which are, in practice, five ways of excommunicating someone by arithmetic. Time asks whether the year 2025 means anything; NoTime removes the reference altogether; and Calendário is the manual of the four clocks, the festivals and the five errors of translation. The Gate — the threshold that decides who enters Route. The city gate with its guardian; the temple gate; the passport; the checkpoint; the login; the paywall; and, in Taoist cultivation texts, the gate as the beginning of the way rather than its obstacle. What it asks. A password, a price, or a category. Every gate converts a person into either a guest or a queue. Hosts. The guard, the border agency, the platform, the hospital triage desk, the receptionist. Where it turns harmful. When the gate cannot be argued with. The three doors of Viragem are a game precisely because all three open; a real gate is the one where one door is locked and the guard will not say why. Prisons and Jail are the gate at its hardest; Habitação is the rent that closes it; Tendas is what remains once it has closed; Aborto is the gate over a body; Rights asks what may be copied at the door; and Poor is the queue at the counter of the transfer. The Tower — the high point that promises safety Route. Babel in Genesis 11; the ziggurat Etemenanki; the cathedral spire; the skyscraper; the central bank; the platform monopoly; the "single source of truth" in a data architecture. What it asks. That everything be visible from one place — which is another way of asking that everything be controlled from one place. Hosts. The king, the firm, the ministry, the cloud provider. Where it turns harmful. Efficiency and fragility are the same property. The tower that sees everything is the tower whose fall confuses every language at once — and the confusion is not linguistic, it is institutional. NATO is global governance as a manual; Geopol plays the same board as a game; CAP-01 and Burocracia are the towers of the market and the ministry; CitizenHelper is the attempt to build one that serves from below; and Abordagem is the doctrine the tower writes for the uniform. The Road — the exile that becomes a category Route. Exodus; the caravan; the pilgrimage, which is a road with a liturgy; the Grand Tour; the refugee route; the nomad camp. The road is the oldest institution for people who have lost the argument at home. What it asks. Hospitality, or a document. The Moral Failure of Biospheric Warfare For millennia, military operations have been conducted within the narrow, delicate band of Earth's atmosphere. This operational paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Conducting war within an inhabited biosphere guarantees the destruction of vital ecosystems, clean water reserves, and arable soil. The resources expended to wage terrestrial warfare directly impair the planetary systems that allow human civilization to endure. Every ordinance detonated on terrestrial ground permanently damages topsoil, releases toxic particulates, and degrades the natural infrastructure required to sustain non-combatant populations. The logic of national defense becomes inherently self-defeating when the methods of defense systematically ruin the land being contested. "To wage war within the ecosystem that generates your own oxygen and food supply is not strategic defense; it is systemic negligence." 02. The Asymmetry of Non-Combatant Harm The primary ethical breakdown of modern terrestrial warfare lies in the unavoidable target overlap between combatants and non-combatants. Despite advances in precision targeting, modern high-yield weaponry cannot isolate military actors from surrounding civilian infrastructure. Children, families, and innocent populations—who possess no formal agency in geopolitical mandates—bear the burden of military engagements. 90% Civilian Casualties in Modern Wars (UN Estimates) 100+ Years of Unexploded Ordnance Risk $2.4T Annual Global Defense Spending Soldiers operate under legal contracts and command hierarchies, fully aware of operational risks. Civilians do not. Confinement of military objectives to populated terrestrial domains represents an ongoing failure to restrict conflict to consenting, professional combatants. 03. Off-Planet Defense as a Logical Pivot If nations insist on maintaining military capabilities, technological deterrence, and strategic competition, logic demands that these operations be relocated entirely outside Earth's atmosphere. The solar system presents an vast, uninhabited operational theater: vacuum environments, dead moons, and unpopulated orbital paths. Redirecting military research, capital, and operational force toward exo-atmospheric domains achieves three critical strategic outcomes: Complete Civilian Isolation: Engagements occurring in vacuum domains eliminate collateral damage to residential zones, civilian infrastructure, and biological ecosystems. Definite Operational Targets: Combat is strictly confined to professional military hardware, automated systems, and specialized personnel. Accelerated Technological Advancement: The extreme environments of space force defense industries to innovate in propulsion, life support, radiation shielding, and material science rather than destructive yield optimization. 04. Re-channeling Technological Imperatives The vast budgets allocated to military research and development must stop serving the architecture of terrestrial ruin. By pivoting defense mandates toward space-based operational capabilities, defense contractors and military engineers will naturally drive humanity's expansion into the solar system. Logistics networks designed for orbital deployment, deep-space communication networks, asteroid resource acquisition, and planetary defense against near-Earth objects represent legitimate uses of organized engineering power. Moving conflict into the void converts destructive potential into the catalyst for species expansion. 05. mistica: Conversas Filosóficas Eu não conhecia o conceito, isto é, o nome que deram ao conceito, mas realmente é interessante. A minha curiosidade anda cada vez menor, há um excesso de informação e conteúdo, que hoje em dia eu já interiorizei, que o melhor na maioria dos casos é simplesmente registar a presença e sem sentir necessidade de entende-la. Estás a conseguir abstrair-te da necessidade de consumir conhecimento de forma compulsiva. Conhecer é bom mas não conhecer também o é. O bom de não conhecer, é que permite-te imaginar (mesmo que a errar) criando uma sensação mística. Essa sensação é interessante, mesmo fazendo parte da “ignorância”. No conteúdo tecnológico, por vezes tenho a impressão que as pessoas não aprendem propriamente nada, mas copia e repete, inttegrando os conceitos que já foram definidos. Também é interessante, principalmente se tencionas criar algo com o conhecimento que tens, mas caso não tenhas essas aspirações, é sem dúvida mais conteúdo que poderá criar “desassossegos”. Não concordo contigo na parte de criar uma “noção mística”. Quero estar em paz com o não conhecer, tendo a consciência disso, preservando-a, sem criar um conhecimento místico ou imaginário para preencher o lugar. Bem pior do que a ignorância é a informação errada. Seria uma discussão para ter, entre a ignorância e a informação errada. Quem é ignorante, significa que não quis aprender sobre um qualquer tema. Quem é errante, significa que quer aprender sobre um qualquer tema. Se nesta vida, para sempre iremos aprender, só quem não erra é que não pode aprender. A ignorância não vem necessariamente de não querer aprender. Em muita coisa que ignoramos nem sequer fomos confrontados com essa possibilidade, simplesmente desconhecemos em absoluto a sua existência. Noutros casos sim, optamos por não saber mais, o que é perfeitamente justificável, face ao tempo finito que dispomos de vida e também, à nossa reduzida capacidade de armazenamento de informação. Aquele que quis aprender sobre algo e fez um esforço válido nesse sentido, pode mesmo assim permanecer ignorante sobre a totalidade da matéria, ou até mesmo errar sobre aquilo que sabe, mas isso é bem diferente de não ter preocupação nenhuma. Não fazer esforço para adquirir conhecimento certo e simplesmente inventar noções místicas sobre o tema. Não discordando, tenho uma opinião diferente quanto à especulação da probabilidade, face ao desconhecimento e ao inexplicável. É que, todo o ser que procurou compreendeer, especulou sobre a probabilidade, sendo que uma maioria terá lido sobre o conteúdo que queria conhecer, os que acabaram por ensinar, aprenderam via essa especulação que inventa probabilidades, como apontadores de verdades. O misticismo não é mais do que essa sensação de estranheza, aquando confrontados com o desconhecido, sendo que a mística é uma disciplina humana, isto é, do foro da sensibilidade humana. Foi assim que a ciência andou durante séculos. Como poderia um cientísta acreditar que a dor expressa pelo cão que está a ser violatado, é uma resposta mecânica e como tal, o animal não sente nem tem emoções? O Big Bang também poderá ser misticismo e especulação, de quem é capaz de imaginar e a partir daí, criar. Novas teorias, verdadeiras ou falsas pouco interessa para esta resposta, mas interessa sim, sublinhar a capacidade de criar a partir do que já conhecia. E por isso, sendo que a teoria do Big Bang é especulatória, ela faz parte da mística, isto é, de uma tentativa de explicar algo que continua a não ter explicação e por isso, entre “deus criou” ou “um atmo explodiu”, ambas as afirmações são verdadeiras e falsas ao mesmo tempo. O que seria da filosofia sem essa tentantiva racional de encontrar uma explicação do abstrato e da realidade? Dai que todas as teorias filosóficas, poderão ser somente especulações, sendo que são apontadores, perspectivas. Por isso, entre a visão puramente racional, que se desliga do ser que sente e que tem capacidade de imaginar e como tal, criar, gosto da perspectiva criativa, que atribuí simbologia e significado ao que já existe como evento, para explicar o que nessa perspectiva criativa, é possível compreender. [Só tentou criar uma explicação criativa, sendo que a puramente racional, também o é, mas a linguagem é mais abstracta do que objectiva. Curiosamente] Uma crença em algo sobrenatural ou misterioso, só porque sim, é diferente da formulação de hipóteses e das posteriores tentativas, feitas para procurar verificar a sua possível validação como a ciência o faz. É claro que a especulação está presente nessa formulação mas são cenários diferentes. O cenário é igual, pois é simplesmente alguém a tentar explicar algo, sendo que a formulação é diferente. Portanto, o que muda é simplesmente a forma de explicar, sendo que nesse aspecto, continuo a gostar das duas formulas. Não é relativo a algo “sobrenatural”, mas natural, que por desconhecimento o torna místerioso. As galáxias e os buracos negros, nada têm de “sobrenatural”, sendo que os efeitos dos seus eventos, cria aos atentos, sensações corporais que traduzem o tal lado “místico”. Pessoalmente relaciono o “místico” ao lado puramente sensorial, isto é, animal, que é também o que somos. Naturalmente que não nego o lado “racional”, sendo esse lado pouco animal. É o que tentamos ser, mas nem sempre somos capazes de ser. Os objectos cãem porque: “Assim quer o Grande Espírito” O potencial desta teoria ser verdadeira é simplísta, mas a formula que a explica é objectiva. Os objectos cãem porque: “…segundo a teoria, explica que..” O potencial desta teoria ser verdadeira é complexa, mas a formula que a explica é subjectiva. … Seja como for, ambas teorias tentam explicar e, com ou sem explicação absoluta, ambas são potencialmente verdadeiras e falsas ao mesmo tempo, tal como o Solipsismo o é. Eu cá gosto de associar as sensações corporais criadas ao ouvir música, com o que é místico. No fundo é o meu cérebro a reagir ao som, que na sua capacidade de imaginar, criam-me sensações. Como não sou eu que estou a crontrolar o meu imaginar, dou-lhe o nome de sensações místicas. Sensações agradáveis ou desagradável, são o resultado de algo que não é controlado por mim, mas pela capacidade de imaginar que o cérebro tem, sem eu ter controlo total, sobre esse efeito. Racionalmente, podes negar essas sensações, mas elas não deixam de existir. E sabe-se que o lado místico tem muitas falácias, mas esse é o lado romântico dos sonhadores. No fundo, é isso que tem graça. É a formula romântica como o lado puramente “místico”, inspirou os que, descreveram um “algo”, que explica “algo mais além desse pequeno algo”. É parte da técnica usada na literatura, não só infantíl. Creio que os textos ciêntificos, também tentam descrever “algo” que explica “algo além desse pequeno algo”, pois o exercício mental é somente comparativo, para sermos capazes de validar a informação. Portanto, o “místico”, tem origem antes de tudo, nos eventos psíquicos dos individuos, que podem leva-lo a tentar explicar a realidade, via a sua sensibilidade e capacidade de imaginar. É um pouco como nos ensinamentos que podemos retirar dos textos. Os ensinamentos antes de aprendidos, são desconhecidos e como tal, místicos. Os ensinamentos também só podem ser aprendidos, caso usemos a lógica, isto é, a auto-comparação da informação. Só assim somos capazes de identificar conteúdos. Eu cá, continuo a gosto do aspecto criativo de como a arte tenta “falar” de conteúdos, sem alguma vez “falar” alguma coisa. Isto é. Só na apreciação do objecto artístico, somos capazes de reconhecer algo que faz parte da peça, como algo que existe previamente em nós. Caso contrário, a peça não poderia criar sensações.

Almost every bad MongoDB schema is a relational schema wearing a JSON costume. MongoDB is a document database. The unit of storage is a BSON document — a binary encoding of an ordered set of field/value pairs that looks like JSON but carries more types. Documents live in collections ; collections live in a database ; a running server process is mongod . There are no tables, no rows, no foreign keys, and no schema enforced by default. instance (mongod) └── database "shop" namespace prefix; auth boundary ├── collection "orders" no fixed schema, per-collection indexes │ ├── document { _id, customer, lines[], total, status } │ ├── document { _id, customer, lines[], total, status } │ └── document { _id, customer, lines[], total, status, refund? } └── collection "customers" └── document { _id, email, addresses[] } A real order document, exactly as you would insert it in Level 5: javascript mongosh · shop.orders copy { _id: ObjectId("66f1c0a2b7d4e91f3c8a1201"), orderNumber: "ORD-2026-000871", customer: { id: ObjectId("66f1b9e0b7d4e91f3c8a1188"), email: "ana.torres@example.com", country: "ES" }, placedAt: ISODate("2026-10-14T09:12:44.318Z"), lines: [ { sku: "KB-88-BRN", name: "Keyboard 88", qty: 1, unitPrice: Decimal128("129.00") }, { sku: "CB-USBC-2M", name: "USB-C cable 2 m", qty: 2, unitPrice: Decimal128("11.50") } ], total: Decimal128("152.00"), currency: "EUR", status: "paid", tags: ["priority", "gift-wrap"], payment: { method: "card", last4: "4242", capturedAt: ISODate("2026-10-14T09:12:51.002Z") } } Everything the application needs to render an order page is in one read. That is the entire point of the model: locality. You are optimising for "fetch the thing I display" instead of "store each fact exactly once". BSON is not JSON BSON adds types JSON lacks, and those types matter operationally. Store money as Decimal128 or integer cents, never as a float; store time as a real date, never as a string. Teams port a normalised schema directly: a users collection, an orders collection, an order_items collection, a products collection. Then every page load fires four queries and joins them in application code, because MongoDB has no JOIN in the CRUD layer. Why it hurts: you pay network round-trips for data that was always displayed together; you lose atomicity across those writes unless you wrap everything in a transaction (which costs more than the relational database you were avoiding); and $lookup at read time cannot use an index on the foreign collection's join key the way a relational planner can. You end up with the drawbacks of both models. What to do instead: decide the access pattern first . If 95% of reads need the order plus its lines, embed the lines. Keep a reference only for data that is large, shared, or updated independently — the product catalogue, not the line item. Level 6 gives you the decision procedure and the five patterns that cover most cases. ✕ Bad decision · "Schemaless means I do not need to design" MongoDB does not enforce a schema by default, so a collection will happily accept {price: "12.00"} in one document and {price: 12} in the next. Every query that compares or sorts on price then behaves inconsistently, and every aggregation that sums it silently skips the string. Why it hurts: the failure is data-dependent, so it appears in production months later, in one shard of your data, and it is not reproducible locally. Type drift is the single most common "MongoDB bug" that is actually a modelling bug. What to do instead: treat the document shape as a contract and enforce it with $jsonSchema validation (Level 6), plus a schema-version field for migrations. "Flexible" should describe your ability to evolve the schema, not the absence of one. If they share a volume with the OS and the OS fills up, mongod stops accepting writes — and a full disk is the most common self-inflicted MongoDB outage after an open port. Path Contents Growth Recommended /var/lib/mongodb Data files ( .wt ), WiredTiger , diagnostic.data Steady, proportional to data + indexes Dedicated XFS volume, noatime /var/log/mongodb mongod.log Slow, but unbounded without rotation Same disk is fine — with rotation /var/backups/mongodb Temporary dumps Spiky, can double your footprint Only as staging; copy off-host /etc/mongod.conf Configuration Bytes Version-controlled (no secrets in it) Table 1.1 — The only four paths that matter. Skip this if /var/lib/mongodb is already on a suitably sized XFS root ; do not invent a volume just to follow along. bash example: /dev/nvme1n1 as the data volume copy # 1. Confirm the device is empty and not mounted. This destroys data. lsblk -f /dev/nvme1n1 # 2. XFS, labelled, mounted with noatime sudo mkfs.xfs -L mongodb-data /dev/nvme1n1 sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/mongodb # 3. On a single-socket VM — most cloud instances — there is nothing to do, and numactl may not even be installed. Open-file limits Every connection costs roughly two file descriptors, and index builds open many files at once. MongoDB's guidance is nofile and nproc of at least 64000 . The official packages ship a systemd unit that sets this, but verify the running process , not your shell: bash after install, in Level 02 copy PID=$(pgrep -x mongod) sudo grep -E 'Max open files|Max processes' /proc/$PID/limits Max open files 64000 64000 files Max processes 64000 64000 processes If those numbers are 1024, add a systemd drop-in (shown in Level 3.6) and restart. This is not theoretical: at 1024 descriptors you fail around 450 connections with Too many open files in the log, and the error looks like a network problem. 1.5 Firewall: default deny, then one hole The application server will connect over the private network. The internet will not. Set the default policy first and open only SSH and — later, restricted — MongoDB. bash ufw copy sudo apt-get -y install ufw sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing sudo ufw allow 22/tcp comment 'ssh' # Allow MongoDB only from the application subnet. Do this in Level 10, # once authentication exists. Level 16 covers graphical clients; they run on your laptop and connect through an SSH tunnel. A desktop environment on a database host is attack surface with no benefit. Separate accounts. Your admin login owns the host; the mongodb OS user (created by the package) owns the data directory and runs mongod . Never run the database as root . Time and logs. UTC everywhere. In the stories I grew up with, the dragon guards the treasure and the monkey learns how to reach it without fighting, which is a much better description of how I work. So when I say monkey, I am not insulting anyone. I am describing the reader who does not accept the first answer, breaks the rule to see what is behind it, and comes back with a joke instead of a wound. What that reference guide is The link above is a collection of notes about security written by another monkey. It is not a course and it is not a product. moreMusicTheory: ◖)) Sound & the Brain A psychology field guide · sound, memory & choice A sound passes. Its meaning can stay. A voice, a song, a warning chime: sound is vibration reaching the ear, but what it means is shaped by a living brain—by attention, learning, memory, emotion, body, culture, and context. 01 From air movement to experience Sound is physical. Hearing is biological. Meaning is interpreted. In air, a sound wave is a traveling pattern of compressions and rarefactions. The air itself does not fly from the source to your ear; local particles oscillate as the pressure disturbance passes. The eardrum and middle-ear bones transmit movement to the fluid-filled cochlea. Hair cells convert that mechanical movement into neural signals, which travel through auditory pathways to the brain. Sound source vibrates → Air pressure wave travels → Ear & cochlea motion becomes neural activity Brain networks analyze patterns ← Context & memory shape interpretation ← Attention selects what matters There is no single “sound meaning” switch. The simplified diagram is a teaching map: auditory processing happens at multiple levels and interacts with attention, expectation, memory, and other brain systems. The physics boundary “Everything vibrates” needs precision Earth is made of matter, and matter can move or oscillate at many scales. The planet can ring in seismic modes after very large earthquakes; molecules in matter also have motion. But that does not mean every object is continuously making audible sound, sharing one special frequency, or responding to sound in the same way. Audible sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium. Earth’s atmosphere carries sound; outer space is mostly vacuum, so ordinary sound does not travel through it as it does through air. Seismic waves in the solid Earth are vibrations too, but they are not the same thing as audible air pressure waves. The psychology boundary A cue can influence—not dictate Brains detect patterns and use learned expectations. A sound may draw attention, signal a likely event, evoke a feeling, or prompt an action. Those are probabilities shaped by situation and learning, not proof that one frequency programs a fixed behavior. People differ. A siren might mean danger to one person, a job to another, and a film scene to someone else. Even for one person, the response may change with safety, context, fatigue, and time. 02 Words have a melody; music has a story How we say something can add information beyond the words themselves. Speech · prosody Voice is more than vocabulary Pitch movement, timing, rhythm, emphasis, loudness, and pauses—together called prosody —help listeners infer emphasis, phrase boundaries, questions, and a speaker’s possible affect. We interpret those cues alongside the actual words and the situation. pitch contour stress timing pauses Music · expectation The brain listens ahead As music unfolds, listeners learn style-specific patterns and form expectations. A continuation, a rhythmic change, or a return may feel rewarding or moving in part because of how it plays with prediction and attention. This is one account of musical pleasure, not a complete explanation for every listener. Familiarity, culture, bodily response, memory, and the moment all contribute too. Emotion · not a decoder ring Recognizing ≠ feeling You can recognize that music sounds sad without feeling sad yourself. A bright voice does not prove happiness; a loud voice does not prove anger. Acoustic cues can inform interpretation, but they are not infallible labels for someone's inner state. Words, context, speaker, listener, and culture change what cues mean. Why a sound can make us laugh—or cry A song linked to a person, place, or past event can act as a retrieval cue. It may bring back a scene, a bodily feeling, or the sense of a particular time in life. A familiar melody can also create emotion through expectation and the way musical events unfold—even without a specific autobiographical memory. These routes may overlap, but no song is guaranteed to evoke the same response in everyone. A vivid memory feels powerful; vividness alone does not certify every detail. Remembering is reconstructive, not a perfect audio-video replay. Emotion can make some aspects memorable while leaving other details uncertain. Treat this as a reason for care—not as a reason to dismiss someone's memory. 03 Memory is a network, not a sound file A cue can reopen a path to associations, but it does not replay the past exactly. A cue can connect several things A familiar sound may become associated with people, places, routines, expectations, and emotions. Hearing it later may retrieve part of that network. What comes to mind depends on the person's history and the present context. SOUND CUE A melody, voice, phrase, alarm, or ambient noise ASSOCIATIONS Where, when, with whom; what was expected RESPONSE Attention, feeling, body response, or action tendency NEW CONTEXT Safety, meaning, and later learning may reshape the response Association isn't destiny Learning can make a once-neutral cue meaningful. A ringtone that repeatedly comes before an important call may grab attention; a song heard during a joyful gathering may become a warm reminder. A cue paired with a distressing event may instead bring unease. These examples describe possible learned links, not a diagnosis. Cues do not affect all people alike, and a learned response can vary or change with later experience. A person's “first choice” is not necessarily a fixed, natural default written by one sound-memory. A sound-triggered reaction can be real without being inevitable, permanent, or fully explained by the sound alone. 04 From sound to behavior: the learning loop A useful chain to notice—not a claim that stimulus automatically causes action. sound / cue → attention & meaning → feeling / body state → possible response → what happens next Learning can connect a cue with what tends to follow. A chime may remind someone to check a message; a beat may invite movement; an alarm may prompt action. Repeated consequences can make a response more likely in a particular context. But a person can notice the cue, interpret it differently, pause, or choose another response. Possible supports Music can help some people feel energized, connected, comforted, or focused in some circumstances. A familiar song may cue autobiographical memories. Rhythm can make movement feel easier or more engaging for some tasks. Possible costs Unwanted or loud noise can interrupt communication, rest, and concentration. Lyrics may compete with reading or verbal memory. A sound associated with threat or loss may be uncomfortable. Effects depend on dose, timing, task, and the person. “Music boosts memory” is too broad. In one study of college students, lyrics impaired tested verbal memory, visual memory, and reading comprehension compared with silence; tested instrumental lo-fi music did not reliably help or harm those tasks. This is a bounded result, not a universal rule about every listener or kind of work. 05 Turn imagination + logic into application A gentle sound-and-response journal. Use a neutral example; skip anything uncomfortable. Private reflection · stays in this page Pick a sound cue and map what you notice. This tool does not record audio, save, or send your entries; refreshing the page clears the form. You do not need to write down personal or upsetting memories. 1 · What kind of sound are you thinking about? A familiar song A spoken phrase A notification or alarm Background noise A rhythm or beat 2 · What do you notice first? (optional) 3 · What is one possible meaning or association? 4 · What small, safe test could help you learn more? Make my reflection card Clear entries Your reflection card will appear here. No answer is scored as good or bad. If a sound or memory feels distressing, stop the exercise, choose a neutral example, or step away. This learning page is not therapy or medical advice. 06 Quick check: observation or overclaim? Choose a response to each statement. Read the feedback, then try the next one. Evidence check Loading question… Careful claim Overclaim Next statement ↗ ↗ Sources & further reading Review articles, research, and public science references behind this manual. OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience — How acoustic information enters the brain University of Minnesota — Auditory pathways to the brain APS / Perspectives on Psychological Science — The Sound of Emotional Prosody Wagner & Watson (2010), Experimental and theoretical advances in prosody: A review Zatorre & Salimpoor (2013), From perception to pleasure: Music and its neural substrates Gold et al. (2019), Musical reward prediction errors engage the nucleus accumbens and motivate learning Salakka et al. (2021), Music evokes autobiographical memories and associated emotions in older adults Schacter (2012), Constructive memory: past and future Kensinger (2009), Remembering the details: Effects of emotion Noba Project — Conditioning and learning Souza & Barbosa (2023), Should we turn off the music? Music with lyrics interferes with cognitive tasks WHO Europe (2018), Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region European Environment Agency (2024), The effect of environmental noise on children OpenStax University Physics — Sound waves NASA — The science of sound Harvard Seismology — Earth’s normal modes Evidence has boundaries: research findings are about specific people, tasks, and conditions. Associations do not by themselves prove cause. This manual offers general education, not a diagnosis, treatment plan, or promise that sound can heal or control behavior.

muttHero: ↶ Home Field Manual MTH-1 · all mail clients suck; this one less mutt — From Nothing to Hero One config file, one key language, IMAP in, SMTP out, several providers at once and colors everywhere. This page is the road: nothing to hero, the four files that matter, and the two hooks (folder-hook, account-hook) that make several mailboxes behave. muttrc · mailboxes · IMAP · SMTP · Gmail vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies passwords stay out of the page and yours 01 From nothing mutt is a terminal email client with a slogan older than the dot-com bubble and still true: “All mail clients suck. This one just sucks less.” It was written in 1995 by Michael Elkins, forked decades later into neomutt , and remains the email program people reach for when they finally want to triage their inbox faster than a pointer can move. It is keyboard-native. Every action is a key; every key is a line in your config. Nothing hidden behind a hamburger. It reads anything. Local mbox, local Maildir, remote IMAP; mutt does not care, which is why it works with any provider's storage. It sends through anything. A local mail server, its own SMTP client, or your provider's submission port — same interface, three backends. It is composable with the rest of the terminal: mutt + w3m for HTML, notmuch for corpus-scale search, your real editor for composing. $ doas pkg_add mutt # BSD-style package naming # Debian/Ubuntu-style: apt install mutt (neomutt is the fork with extra patches) Note: vanilla mutt and neomutt share the config language; this page exists in both worlds and every line below opens in both. Where a feature is fork-only, the page says so — and those are extras, not the road. 02 First mail, first keys Start mutt against something real. If you have mail lying in a local Maildir already: $ mutt -f ~/Mail/INBOX # open a specific mailbox $ mutt -y # open the mailbox browser (see section 04) And the first keyboard vocabulary — small, and it never changes: Key Moves j / k (and arrows) Down / up through messages or entries. <Enter> Open the message (pager view). q Close current view (pager → index; index → quit). c Change mailbox (see = and ? expansion below). d / u Mark deleted / undelete (a D in the index; real purge at exit). s Save message to a mailbox (copy+delete in one move). r / g / L Reply / group (all) reply / list reply. v View attachments of the message. ? Show the whole key map in this context. Use it; it is a manual living inside the program. Note: in mailbox-name prompts, = expands to your folder value ( =Sent is ~/Mail/Sent ) and ! is your spoolfile . That shorthand is why config lines below look so short. 03 The configuration files mutt reads, in order: /etc/Muttrc (or /etc/muttrc ) — the system-wide base; you rarely touch it. ~/.muttrc (or ~/.config/mutt/muttrc ) — everything of yours lives here. Any other file you source from those two — and that is where multi-account life (section 05) comes from. The nothing-to-something core, six lines, no account yet: # ~/.muttrc — the spine set mbox_type = Maildir # maildir > mbox: one file per message set folder = ~/Mail # the root all =names expand into set spoolfile = =INBOX # the default mailbox mutt opens set record = =Sent # copies of what you send set postponed = =Drafts # where postponed drafts live And create the Maildir directories on disk (a shell line, not a mutt line): $ mkdir -p ~/Mail/INBOX ~/Mail/Sent ~/Mail/Drafts ~/Mail/Archive Note: to check your own bindings at any time: ? in the compose screen shows that context's key map, and :set ?postponed echoes the value of a variable. Between those two answers, no config question stays unanswered while mutt is open. Warn: do not copy a stranger's 900-line muttrc before you have your own six lines working. Borrowed configs are how people end up mutt users with no idea why mail moves. Grow yours sideways (sections 04–09), one block at a time. 04 One box, many mailboxes The multi-email box starts with a declaration: which mailboxes exist and which show in the browser. Then every folder gets its own behaviour: # ~/.muttrc — declare the landscape mailboxes =INBOX =Sent =Drafts =Archive mailboxes =lists/mutt # lists live in a subtree, declared like the rest # behaviour per folder folder-hook . "set sort=threads" # everywhere: threads folder-hook =lists.* "set sort=date-received" # lists: pure chronology Note the honest limit: mutt does not create folders for you on disk; the mkdir from section 03 done once is why =INBOX resolves. The browser mutt -y opens a list of every mailboxes line with unread counts. Move with j / k , open with Enter ; same keys as everywhere. New folders? Add one mailboxes line; the browser follows. Note: Maildir folders are directories of files, so you can point any plaintext tool at them while mutt has them open. That property is the quiet superpower of the storage format (and the reason mbox gets dropped by everyone who survives a crash once). 05 Many accounts, one muttrc The multi-account pattern is one account-hook (fires when the account is selected) plus per-account files laid out like documents, sourced by the spine: # ~/.muttrc — the hub account-hook $fastmail "source ~/.mutt/fastmail.conf" account-hook $workmail "source ~/.mutt/work.conf" folder-hook fastmail.com.* "source ~/.mutt/fastmail.hooks" folder-hook work.example.com.* "source ~/.mutt/work.hooks" mailboxes ! "imaps://imap.fastmail.com/INBOX" "imaps://imap.work.example.com/INBOX" Each account file carries its own identity, server pair and signature, and declares its own set lines — a mini-section-03, plus the network pair of sections 06–07: # ~/.mutt/fastmail.conf — account template set from = "you@fastmail.com" set realname = "Your Name" set imap_user = "you@fastmail.com" set imap_pass = "" empty = prompt; see the gpg line below set folder = "imaps://imap.fastmail.com/" set smtp_url = "smtps://you@fastmail.com@mail.messagingengine.com" set signature = "~/.mutt/signature.fm" # secrets, decrypted at machine startup — never committed anywhere source "gpg -q --for-your-eyes-only --no-tty -d ~/.mutt/fastmail.gpg |" Warn: account-hook fires on operations (opening a folder, sending), not at startup. If both accounts share secrets in plain set lines, the last file sourced wins at the worst moment. The fix is discipline: per-account files, sourced by hook, never by the spine directly. Where do passwords belong? Not in the file you keep in git. Either way, one thing stays out of the muttrc you keep in git: the password. The classic is a gpg-decrypt-in-flight source "gpg -d ~/.mutt/secrets.gpg |" line that sets imap_pass and smtp_pass at startup; otherwise mutt will simply prompt you, per account, per session.. 06 IMAP: reading from a distance Point folder at an imap(s):// URL and mutt becomes an IMAP client: the mailbox browser lists folders straight off the server, and = names still expand against it. # ~/.muttrc — IMAP core set imap_user = "you@example.com" set imap_pass = "" # empty = prompt; or sourced from gpg set folder = "imaps://imap.example.com/" mailboxes =INBOX "imaps://imap.example.com/OtherFolder" The server-politeness knobs, safe as written: set imap_check_subscribed = yes # trust the server's folder list set mail_check = 60 # imap poll interval, seconds set imap_peek = yes # do NOT auto-mark as read on list set imap_keepalive = 300 # keep NAT/freewalls open during long reads Note: first connect to a new server prints a certificate prompt — read it (fingerprints are the whole point of TLS), accept once, and it is cached. If your provider's certificate chain is normal, this is a once-per-machine moment. 07 SMTP: sending without fear mutt can hand finished mail to your provider directly, skipping any local MTA: # ~/.muttrc — direct submission set smtp_url = "smtps://you@example.com@mail.example.com:465" set smtp_pass = "" # prompt or gpg, like imap_pass set from = "You <you@example.com>" unset write_bcc # do not leak Bcc to the wire; server handles it smtps:// = implicit TLS on port 465 . smtp://...:587 = STARTTLS on the submission port. Prefer smtps when a provider offers both; both are fine. If smtp_url is unset, mutt falls back to the local sendmail -compatible binary — and that is the second, classic route: # ~/.muttrc — delegate delivery to msmtp (config lives in ~/.msmtprc) set sendmail = "/usr/bin/msmtp" Note: pick one route per account and leave the other unset. When both are configured, debugging "why did this mail take the weird path" becomes a zebra hunt. The direct smtp_url route is the one this page recommends for laptops; the sendmail route belongs on the server that already has an MTA. 08 Providers, Gmail included Provider recipes are thin layers over what sections 06–07 already taught. Three common ones: Provider IMAP folder SMTP KVR (ligatório read) Gmail imaps://imap.gmail.com/INBOX smtps://smtp.gmail.com:465 Gmail wraps IMAP in labels; special folders are literally [Gmail]/ -prefixed. Fastmail imaps://imap.fastmail.com/ smtps://mail.messagingengine.com Plain IMAP service; server-side Sent tracked by your record . Any ISP / work server imaps://imap.example.com/INBOX smtps://mail.example.com Same three lines; differences are only the values and the names server-side. Gmail, the whole truth # ~/.mutt/gmail.conf set from = "you@gmail.com" set imap_user = "you@gmail.com" set folder = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/" set spoolfile = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/INBOX" set record = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/[Gmail]/Sent Mail" set trash = "imaps://imap.gmail.com/[Gmail]/Trash" set smtp_url = "smtps://you@gmail.com@smtp.gmail.com:465" set imap_check_subscribed = yes set imap_list_subscribed = yes And the three truths of the label reality (because Gmail is IMAP-wrapped, not native IMAP): Labels are not folders. A message lives in [Gmail]/All Mail and may also appear under any label. mutt browses labels as if they were folders, but deleting manipulates labels, not atoms. Delete means archive or trash — your choice. With trash set above, plain d respects the Trash. For real archive behaviour add a macro that saves to [Gmail]/Archive instead. Decide once; both are one line. Sent lives server-side. Gmail's web UI auto-files every send; point your record at [Gmail]/Sent Mail and both worlds will agree by pointing at the same place. Authentication is its own paragraph, because Gmail is the most common wall: normal password login requires an app password when 2FA is enabled (it should be). The app password is generated in the provider's security settings and behaves like a normal password string, which makes it a perfect fit for the gpg-sourced file from section 05. Warn: do not keep 2FA-disabled mail accounts "just for mutt" no matter how convenient; the app password path is the supported one. Also note that a bare mutt without IMAP+SMTP support compiled in (check mutt -v ) cannot talk to any provider here — your package choice matters. Warn: do not ever keep 2FA-disabled Gmail accounts "just for mutt". The app password path is the supported one; a 2FA-less account is a weaker target, and your inbox is the key to every other account you own. 09 Colors like a command line deserves mutt colors objects , not widgets: bundles such as normal , hdrdefault , quoted , signature , indicator , index . Syntax: color OBJECT foreground background [pattern] , with default meaning "terminal's own". # ~/.muttrc — a complete, calm, dark start color normal white default color hdrdefault cyan default color quoted green default color quoted1 brightgreen default color signature blue default color attachment yellow default color search black brightyellow color indicator black brightgreen color status white blue color tilde brightwhite default color tree magenta default color error red default color message white green color markers red default All of those, as they would land on your dark terminal (CSS speaking for the terminal palette): normal hdrdefault quoted signature attachment indicator status error And the two object+pattern powers that separate a scheme from decoration: # unread messages scream softly color index brightwhite default "~N" # your own outgoing mail, dimmed color index blue default "~P!~F" Note: 256-color identifiers also work ( color normal color252 default ); default keeps the terminal's own. Test choices by eye, live, with :color ... typed straight into the pager — no reload ritual required: it is what resource files wish they were. 10 Patterns: the search superpower l (limit) collapses the index to a sub-world;Everything else — color, hook, save, archive — reuses the same small grammar: Pattern Means Example limit ~N new/unread l ~N → only what waits for you ~f user@host from l ~f butter@club.tld ~t user@host to (you included) l ~t me@tld ~s words subject contains l ~s "invoice" ~F / ~D flagged / deleted l ~F !pattern negation — "does not match" l !~s "cron" & , | , (...) Boolean and / or / grouping l (~N & ~f boss@work.tld) Where it earns with interest: color index ... pattern — the colors in section 09 are pattern-driven. T (tag-pattern) + ; (apply next command to tagged) turns inbox-zero into arithmetic, not patience: one pattern, everything matching, one key, ruined in bulk or filed in bulk. The same notation is mutt's single search language; there is no second one to learn for hooks, colors, limits and tags — which is rare and lovely. Note: the full grammar lives in muttrc(5) , under "Patterns". Keep that man page handy; it is the accidental second manual for the whole program. 11 Keys and macros worth stealing mutt has bind (one key, one named function) and macro (one key, a symphony of virtual keypresses). The handful worth more than their line-count: # ~/.muttrc — quality of life (mutt 1.11+ has the sidebar built in) set sidebar_visible = yes set sidebar_width = 24 # b toggles the sidebar in both index and pager macro index,pager b "<enter-command>set sidebar_visible=!sidebar_visible<enter>" # Tab jumps to the next mailbox with unseen mail bind index \Ct <sidebar-next> # one key to archive: save to =Archive, mark deleted in place macro index,pager a "<save-message>=Archive<enter><delete-message>" # G runs fetchmail-style helpers, if you have one; delete the line if you do not macro index G "<shell-escape>fetchmail</shell-escape><refresh>" Note: the purpose of the macros above is to teach the shape: macro context keys "actions" , actions as if typed in the interface wrapped in <...> function names. Start by simulating your last three manual actions; that is the macro list you actually need, custom-made by your own hands. Warn: two macro-writers' hazards: what genuinely bites is shadowing a default key you use without remembering (bind b away and mutt will never warn), and a macro that fires the wrong context because you forgot the index,pager prefix. Gate 1 6 questions ~50 min 1.1 What a network is A network is a group of devices that have agreed on how to encode bits on a medium , how to identify each other , and how to decide who speaks next . That is the whole trick. Every protocol in this manual is a formal answer to one of those three problems, plus the policy layer humans add on top: who is allowed to talk to whom. Two laptops on a desk with one cable between them are a network. So is a data centre with 40,000 servers. The difference is scale, and scale forces hierarchy: you cannot have 40,000 devices all hearing every message, so you introduce addressing, segmentation, and routing. Routing is how a network grows beyond what one device can remember. Mental model Think of a parcel. The street address is the IP address: it describes a location in a hierarchy that routers understand. The name on the door is the MAC address: it identifies the specific network card on the local segment. The courier’s route plan is the routing table. The packing slip is the transport header. If any one of those is wrong, the parcel does not arrive — and the tracking information lies to you in a different way each time. There are two big families of delivery you need to keep separate in your head: Connection-oriented (TCP): a phone call. You establish it, you acknowledge what you hear, you retransmit what was lost, you close it. Reliability has a cost: state, memory, and delay. Connectionless (UDP, IP itself): a postcard. Fire and forget. Cheaper and faster; the application decides whether loss matters. DNS queries, voice, and video generally prefer this. 1.2 Layers and encapsulation The OSI model is a teaching taxonomy with seven layers; the TCP/IP model is what the Internet actually implements, usually drawn with four or five. Neither is physics. Their value is diagnostic: when something breaks, layers tell you which question to ask next and stop you from “rebooting the firewall” because a cable is unplugged. Figure 1-1 · OSI layers mapped to real protocols, devices, and troubleshooting questions # Layer PDU Protocols / addresses Typical device Question it answers 7 Application Data HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH Server, proxy What does the user want? 6 Presentation Data TLS, JSON, ASN.1, encoding — How is it represented? 5 Session Data SMB sessions, RPC, TLS session — Who is still talking? 4 Transport Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) TCP, UDP, ports Firewall (L4) Which application, and did it arrive? 3 Network Packet IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, OSPF, BGP Router, L3 switch Where does it need to go? 2 Data link Frame Ethernet, 802.1Q, ARP, PPP Switch, NIC, AP Who on this local link gets it? 1 Physical Bits / symbols 1000BASE-T, 10GBASE-SR, Wi-Fi RF Cable, SFP, antenna Can a signal get there at all? Encapsulation is the nested-envelope effect. Each layer adds a header (and sometimes a trailer) and hands the whole thing down. The receiving side strips them in reverse. The key consequence: a router normally cares only down to Layer 3, and a switch only down to Layer 2 . Each one rewrites a different envelope. The source host puts the gateway’s MAC on the frame, not the server’s. Every router along the path strips the old frame and builds a new one. The server’s address is 93.184.216.34 (a real address historically used by example.com; documentation ranges are used elsewhere in this manual). The frame format you meet most often is Ethernet II: Figure 1-4 · Ethernet II frame — 64 bytes minimum, 1518 bytes maximum without VLAN tag Field Bytes Purpose Preamble + SFD 7 + 1 Clock synchronisation; not counted in frame size Destination MAC 6 Unicast, broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff), or multicast Source MAC 6 The transmitting NIC EtherType 2 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x8100 802.1Q tag, 0x0806 ARP Payload 46–1500 The encapsulated packet, padded if smaller than 46 FCS 4 CRC-32. Bad FCS → frame dropped silently The MTU is the largest payload an interface will send: 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet. That 1500 includes the IP header, so a TCP segment typically carries 1460 bytes of application data (1500 − 20 IP − 20 TCP) before options. A VLAN tag adds 4 bytes, so a tagged frame can be 1522 bytes on the wire while the IP MTU stays 1500. Jumbo frames (9000) exist in storage and data-centre fabrics but must be configured consistently end to end; one 1500-byte hop in the path silently breaks them. Classic outage Path MTU discovery relies on ICMP “fragmentation needed” (Type 3, Code 4). A firewall that blocks all ICMP creates an MTU black hole : small requests work, large responses hang forever. The symptom is famous — a website loads halfway, SSH connects and then freezes after login, VPN tunnels establish but no data passes. Fix the ICMP policy, or clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel, rather than lowering MTU on random hosts. Copper twisted pair (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a) is cheap and limited to about 100 m for standard Ethernet. Fibre (multimode OM3/OM4 for buildings, single-mode OS2 for long haul) carries far more bandwidth over kilometres. What matters operationally: the optic must match the fibre, the wavelength, and the reach . A 10GBASE-LR optic will not light up over multimode patch leads, no matter how confident the installer is. Duplex is the other silent killer. Full duplex means both sides can transmit simultaneously; half duplex means one at a time. Modern switched Ethernet is full duplex everywhere, and gigabit requires autonegotiation for duplex. When one side is hard-coded full and the other auto-negotiates, the auto side falls back to half — a duplex mismatch . The full-duplex side transmits whenever it wants; the half-duplex side detects “collisions” that are really the other side talking. Result: late collisions, CRC/FCS errors, terrible throughput, and a link that reports “up”. The fix is boring: set both ends to speed auto / duplex auto , or hard-code both to the same values. Never hard-code one end only. And note that late collisions on a link that is supposed to be full duplex is not a cable problem — it is a configuration problem. 1.5 MAC addresses and ARP A MAC address is 48 bits, written as six hex octets. The first three bytes are the OUI (vendor), the last three are assigned by the vendor. The least significant bit of the first octet distinguishes unicast from multicast; the second-least significant bit marks a locally administered address (common in virtual machines and privacy features). Broadcast is all ones: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff . ARP (Address Resolution Protocol, RFC 826 ) glues IPv4 to Ethernet. A host that needs to send to 192.168.10.1 on its own subnet broadcasts “Who has 192.168.10.1? Tell 192.168.10.10”, and the owner replies with its MAC. The result is cached for a few minutes. For a destination off the subnet, the host ARPs for the gateway , then puts the gateway’s MAC on the frame with the server’s IP inside. ARP has no authentication . Any host can answer “that IP is me” and begin receiving traffic meant for the gateway. That is ARP spoofing, and it is the foundation of most on-path attacks in a flat LAN. Level 05 covers the defences (Dynamic ARP Inspection, DHCP snooping, port security, segmentation). For now, remember the design flaw: the protocol trusts whoever speaks first . IPv6 does not use ARP. Neighbor Discovery (ND, RFC 4861 ) uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, with Duplicate Address Detection built in. It is still unauthenticated by default; SEND (RFC 3971) exists but is rarely deployed, so ND spoofing is just as real. 1.6 What a switch really does A switch is a Layer 2 bridge with many ports. It learns source MAC addresses into a CAM table (content-addressable memory), then forwards frames destined to a known MAC only out that port. Unknown destination, broadcast, and multicast frames are flooded to all ports in the same VLAN. That is the whole algorithm, and almost every Layer 2 mystery is a consequence of it. Learn — source MAC plus ingress port goes into the table, with an ageing timer (300 seconds by default on Cisco). Forward — destination MAC is known and not on the ingress port: send only there. Flood — destination is unknown, broadcast, or multicast: send everywhere in the VLAN except the source port. Filter — destination is on the same port it arrived from (common with hubs or a shared segment): drop. A collision domain is the set of devices that share a medium and can collide. A switch gives each port its own collision domain. A broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive each other’s broadcast frames; by default, one VLAN equals one broadcast domain. A router (or a Layer 3 interface) is the boundary between broadcast domains. If you remember only one sentence about switches: they extend broadcast domains and break collision domains . MAC flooding attacks exploit the CAM table: send thousands of frames with random source MACs until the table is full, and the switch falls back to flooding everything, letting the attacker capture traffic. nodeSecurity: Node.js Paranoid Security on Debian: Own The Server, Expose Nothing Mindset: you own the server, so you distrust everything else — code, packages, users, bots, even yourself at 2am. Application below: a tiny secure notes API ( Node.js + Express ) behind Nginx on Debian 12 . Every tip is obsessive on purpose. If it feels excessive, good — attackers are excessive. 0 — The App We Harden (So Tips Have Teeth) Stack: Node.js 20 LTS ( nodejs.org ), Express 4 ( expressjs.com ), PostgreSQL 15 ( postgresql.org ) or SQLite for tiny, Nginx ( nginx.org ) reverse proxy, PM2 or systemd ( pm2 ), Debian 12 Bookworm ( debian.org ), UFW/nftables ( Debian nftables ), Fail2ban ( fail2ban.org ), Certbot ( certbot.eff.org ). PARANOID RULE #1: never commit .env . Ever. .env in git = public secret. Add to .gitignore day zero, rotate any key that touched git history with Gitleaks . node --version # v20.x project/ server.js routes/ middleware/ .env (600, root:www-data? NO — app user only) .gitignore -> .env, node_modules, *.log, *.pem 1 — Debian Base: Minimal, Updated, Boring (Boring = Safe) Install minimal Debian, no desktop. Create deploy user, kill root SSH. Tip in spirit: if you don't need it, uninstall it. apt update && apt full-upgrade -y apt install -y unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges sudo ufw fail2ban unattended-upgrades useradd -m -s /bin/bash deploy usermod -aG sudo deploy # /etc/ssh/sshd_config: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, AllowUsers deploy systemctl restart ssh ufw default deny incoming; ufw default allow outgoing ufw allow 22/tcp; ufw allow 80/tcp; ufw allow 443/tcp; ufw enable # auto security updates: dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades ✔ Enable unattended-upgrades for security only. Full auto-upgrade can break Node; security-only + weekly manual apt full-upgrade in maintenance window. Links: Debian UnattendedUpgrades , Debian SSH , Debian Security . 2 — .env & Secrets: The Crown Jewels (Treat Like Nuclear Codes) PARANOID RULE #2: .env lives once, on server, chmod 600, owned by app user. No backups to Dropbox. No Slack pastes. No console.log(process.env) . # /opt/notesapp/.env — chmod 600, chown notesapp:notesapp PORT=127.0.0.1:3000 DATABASE_URL=postgres://notesapp:'S0mething-Long-32chars'@127.0.0.1:5432/notes SESSION_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) # load with dotenv ONLY in dev; in prod use systemd EnvironmentFile npm i dotenv # https://www.npmjs.com/package/dotenv Better than .env on your own server: systemd EnvironmentFile=/etc/notesapp/env (600 root, read at start, never in repo), or HashiCorp Vault ( vaultproject.io ) / SOPS ( mozilla/sops ) for rotation. Validate at boot with dotenv-safe or Zod — crash if SESSION_SECRET < 32 chars . ✔ Scan repo pre-commit with Gitleaks + git-secrets . Add .env.example with fake values only. 3 — Node App Hardening: Headers, Limits, Injection-Proof npm i express helmet cors express-rate-limit express-mongo-sanitize xss-clean hpp cookie-parser csurf jsonwebtoken bcrypt pg zod # https://www.npmjs.com/package/helmet — sets 11+ secure headers // server.js — paranoid skeleton const helmet = require('helmet'); app.disable('x-powered-by'); app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"] } }, hsts: { maxAge: 31536000, includeSubDomains: true, preload: true } })); app.use(express.json({ limit: '10kb' })); // no 10MB JSON bombs const limiter = require('express-rate-limit')({ windowMs: 15*60*1000, max: 100, standardHeaders: true }); app.use('/api/', limiter); // auth: bcrypt cost 12, jwt 15min + refresh rotate, httpOnly SameSite=Strict Secure cookies // validate every input with zod; parameterize SQL (pg $1); no string concat PARANOID RULE #3: trust no input — not body, query, header, file, webhook. OWASP NodeJS Cheat Sheet is bedtime reading. Deps: npm audit; npm audit fix , automate with Grype / Snyk / Dependabot . Pin with package-lock.json , npm ci --omit=dev in prod. Never npm install as root. 4 — Run As Nobody: systemd, Non-Root, Read-Only Where Possible # /etc/systemd/system/notesapp.service [Service] User=notesapp Group=notesapp WorkingDirectory=/opt/notesapp EnvironmentFile=/etc/notesapp/env ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /opt/notesapp/server.js Restart=always NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateTmp=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true ReadWritePaths=/opt/notesapp/logs AmbientCapabilities= # UMask=0077 so logs 600 ✔ App binds 127.0.0.1:3000 only. World talks to Nginx , never Node directly. ss -tlnp must show Node on localhost. 5 — Nginx Shield: TLS, No Leaks, No .env Ever Served Nginx docs , Mozilla SSL config . server { listen 443 ssl http2; server_name api.example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/privkey.pem; add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always; add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always; add_header Referrer-Policy no-referrer always; client_max_body_size 1m; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr; } location ~ /\. { deny all; } # block .env, .git location ~* \.(env|pem|key|sql|bak)$ { deny all; } } # certbot --nginx -d api.example.com (https://certbot.eff.org/) # test: curl -I https://api.example.com/.env must be 403/404, never 200 PARANOID RULE #4: static root never contains code. root /var/www/public holds only built assets. .git never deployed — deploy tarball via rsync --exclude='.git --exclude=.env' . 6 — Data: Postgres Locked Down, Backups Encrypted # Postgres listens localhost only, scram-sha-256, least privilege: # /etc/postgresql/15/main/postgresql.conf: listen_addresses='127.0.0.1' # pg_hba.conf: host notes notesapp 127.0.0.1/32 scram-sha-256 CREATE USER notesapp WITH PASSWORD 'long-random'; CREATE DATABASE notes OWNER notesapp; REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE notes FROM PUBLIC; # backups: pg_dump | gpg --encrypt | restic to offsite (https://restic.net/) Encrypt backups with GnuPG , store keys offline. Test restore quarterly. Log with pgaudit for sensitive tables. 7 — Perimeter: Fail2ban, Monitoring, No Phone-Home # fail2ban jail for nginx + ssh (http://www.fail2ban.org/) [nginx-limit-req] enabled=true [sshd] maxretry=3 bantime=1h # logs: journalctl + logrotate, 600 perms, ship to local Loki (https://grafana.com/oss/loki/) — no third-party loggers with secrets # monitor: Uptime Kuma (https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma) self-hosted, AIDE (https://aide.github.io/) integrity ✔ Run Lynis audit monthly. Redact secrets from logs: logLevel warn , never log tokens, mask with pino-noir ( pino-noir ). 8 — Deploy Checklist (Copy-Paste Paranoia) ☐ .env 600, not in git, Gitleaks clean ☐ npm ci --omit=dev, npm audit clean ☐ helmet + rate-limit + zod validation + parameterized SQL ☐ systemd non-root + NoNewPrivileges + binds localhost ☐ Nginx TLS + security headers + deny .env/.git ☐ UFW deny-all + Fail2ban + unattended-upgrades ☐ Postgres localhost + scram + encrypted restic backups ☐ curl tests: /.env=403, /api without token=401, big JSON=413 ☐ headers check: securityheaders.com + ssllabs.com/ssltest Verify: securityheaders.com , SSL Labs , OWASP Cheatsheets .
